title: Why a Full Retainer Book Doesn't Mean a Profitable Marketing Agency
linkedin:
A full retainer book feels like proof everything is working. For a lot of marketing and creative agencies, it isn't.

We keep seeing the same pattern in owner-led agencies. Utilisation looks healthy on the timesheet, the studio is busy, retainers renew, clients are happy. But profit at month end never quite matches how busy the year has felt.

The gap usually lives inside the retainer accounts themselves. An extra revision round here, a same-day request there, a small brand tweak folded in because it felt too minor to raise formally. None of it feels like giving away margin in the moment.

Compounded over a year, that pattern can quietly shift an account from comfortably profitable to break-even, without the fee ever changing and without anyone noticing the exact point it happened.

The only way to catch it is to look at profitability account by account, not at total agency revenue. The client generating the most billings is often the one absorbing the most unbilled scope, simply because a bigger account creates more surface area for one-off requests to pile up.

Once that's visible, the fix is rarely dramatic. It is a scope conversation, not a price fight, walking the client through what the retainer originally covered against what is now being delivered.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

A note for local business owners, especially those running marketing, creative or media agencies across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria.

A full retainer book and a busy studio feel like proof that things are going well. Often the profit numbers tell a different story, and the reason usually isn't one bad client, it's small additions that build up over time. An extra revision round, a same-day request, a small tweak folded into the retainer because raising it formally felt like too much fuss.

None of these moments look like giving away margin on their own. Over a year, though, they can shift an account from properly profitable to barely break-even without the fee ever changing.

The only reliable way to catch this is to look at each client's profitability on its own, rather than relying on total revenue, since the busiest account is often not the most profitable one once the real time behind it is counted.
